entries.explanation: Write a backslash followed by neg for negation.
Use land between the two statements joined by and.
Use lor between statements joined by or.
Use to for a right-pointing implication arrow.
Use leftrightarrow for the two-direction arrow.
Use equiv for the equivalence symbol.
Use therefore for the three-dot therefore symbol.
Use vdash for the turnstile symbol.

Rightarrow draws a double implication arrow, another way to write “if p, then q.” This is a typography variant of the implication arrow used above, not the two-way biconditional. The capital R matters.
Use Longrightarrow for this arrow variant; capitalization matters. Its meaning follows the lesson convention.
Use Longleftrightarrow for this arrow variant; capitalization matters. Its meaning follows the lesson convention.
Use forall for the upside-down A.
Use exists for the backward E.
Use in for membership.
Put the letter inside braces after mathbb to make a blackboard-bold letter. A single-letter argument may omit braces, as in \mathbb Z, but using braces consistently makes the grouping clearer.
Use notin for nonmembership.
Use subseteq for the subset-or-equal symbol.
Use subset for the subset symbol; follow the mathematical convention stated in the lesson.
Use subsetneq for proper containment.
Use nsubseteq for not a subset.
Use cup for union.
Use cap for intersection.
Use setminus for set difference.
Use varnothing for the empty-set symbol.
Put a capital letter inside braces after mathcal for a calligraphic letter. A single capital letter can omit braces, as in \mathcal P; braces are recommended for clarity.
Use bigcup with underscore and caret groups for the indexed union limits.
Use bigcap with underscore and caret groups for the indexed intersection limits.
Use mid for the divisibility bar.
Use nmid for the crossed divisibility bar.
Put the modulus inside braces after pmod; it adds the parenthesized mod label. A single-character modulus can omit braces, as in \pmod4. A multi-digit modulus needs braces, as in \pmod{12}.
Use preceq for the curved order symbol with an equality bar.
Use prec for the strict curved order symbol.
Use mapsto for the arrow with a vertical bar at its tail.
Use circ for the composition symbol. Here S and R name relations: S after R, in the order explained above. Later, the same command also types function composition.
Pair lfloor with rfloor for floor brackets.
Use rfloor to close the floor brackets.
Pair lceil with rceil for ceiling brackets.
Use rceil to close the ceiling brackets.
Use sum followed by a lower group after underscore and an upper group after caret.
Use prod with lower and upper groups for a product.
Use ldots for three baseline dots.
Use cdots for three centered dots.
Give frac two brace groups: numerator first, denominator second.

Put the expression under the radical inside braces after sqrt; an optional [3] before the group makes a cube root. A single-character argument can omit braces, as in \sqrt y. Use braces to put a whole sum under the radical, as in \sqrt{y+1}.
Use cdot for a centered multiplication dot.

Use times for the cross. Here A and B are sets and the cross means their Cartesian product, as defined above. Between numbers it can instead mean multiplication; the command draws the symbol, while the surrounding objects determine its meaning.
Use leq for less than or equal to.
Use geq for greater than or equal to.
Use ne for not equal.
neq is an alternative spelling of ne.
Use pm for plus-or-minus.
Use infty for the infinity symbol.

Use log for an upright function name and underscore for its base. Type \log_2 n for log base two of n, or \log_{10}(n+1) for a multi-character base and a compound argument. Keep the entire base in its subscript group and put the argument after it. Writing log without a backslash would display three separate italic letters.
Use max for an upright function name.
Use gcd for an upright function name.

Give binom two brace groups: the top entry first and the bottom entry second. For example, \binom{10}{3} prints ten choose three. Each group may be omitted only for a single character, which is why the text may show \binom93 for nine choose three. Keep braces for multi-digit numbers and expressions such as n-1; \binom103 would use 1 and 0 as its two entries and leave 3 outside.
Use rho for the lowercase Greek letter rho.
Use ell for the script-style lowercase l.
Use varepsilon for the curly epsilon form.
Capitalization matters: Theta produces capital theta.
Capitalization matters: Omega produces capital omega.
star prints a star. It can be a superscript label, as in x^{\star}. A star has no fixed mathematical meaning here: an author must explain what a starred label denotes.
Use triangle for the triangle symbol; its meaning comes from the lesson.
Put ordinary words inside braces after text. Spaces inside that group are retained, so a label can appear within a mathematical expression.
Put letters in braces after mathrm to make them upright, as in the truth-value label T. This changes lettering, not mathematical meaning.
Put a custom function name inside braces after operatorname.
Put a symbol inside mathbin to give it binary-operator spacing.
Use deg for the upright degree label.
Use left before an opening delimiter and right before its closing partner to size them together.
Use right before the closing delimiter paired with left.
Use bigl before the opening delimiter of a manually enlarged pair.
Use bigr before the closing delimiter of a manually enlarged pair.
quad inserts a visible space in math.
qquad inserts twice the space of quad.
A backslash followed by a comma inserts a thin space.
Escape a brace with a backslash when you want it printed rather than used for grouping.
Escape the closing brace with a backslash when you want it printed.
Two backslashes start a new row inside a supported multirow environment.
Start an environment with begin and its name in braces; use ampersands between columns.
Close an environment with end and the same name in braces.
Escape a dollar sign to print it without opening or closing math.
Escape percent to print a percent sign.
Escape an underscore to print it instead of starting a subscript.
Escape an ampersand to print it instead of separating columns.
Escape a hash sign to print it, for example as an ordinary item-number label. It has no special counting meaning in this example.
A backslash followed by a space inserts an explicit space in mathematics. Ordinary spaces usually do not affect mathematical spacing.
Use cos for the cosine function; theta names the angle.
Use theta for the Greek angle label theta. Its meaning is supplied by the lesson.
Use lambda for the Greek letter naming an eigenvalue.
Use uppercase Sigma for the SVD diagonal matrix. This is a letter, unlike the sum command that inserts a summation operator.
Use a backslash followed by a vertical bar on each side for double norm bars. The bars denote Euclidean length in these lessons.
Use det for determinant. For a two-by-two matrix with rows (a,b),(c,d), this scalar is ad-bc. A zero value means the matrix is not invertible.
Lowercase sigma names an individual singular value. A subscript labels which value. Uppercase \Sigma names the entire rectangular diagonal matrix; TeX is case-sensitive.
